title: General era tells
about: The baseline: the clues that date almost any photo, whatever is in it.
sheet: Glass-plate black & white, very sharp, stiff posing, long exposure blur of moving people
Kodachrome saturated colour (reds, blues) in professional or travel shots
Warm, faded, orange/yellow colour cast, soft grain
Flash-lit snapshots, red-eye, date stamp in orange digits in the corner
Early digital: low resolution, blown-out skies, purple fringing
Sharp HDR phone photos, wide-angle, portrait-mode blur
Phones in hands: flip phones 2000–2007, smartphones 2009+
Earbuds with white cable 2003–2016, wireless AirPods 2017+
Trams and trolley wires everywhere in western cities; removed in many US/UK/French cities 1950s–60s
Gas lamps → electric streetlights; sodium orange lights 1960s–2000s; white LED lights 2010s+
Soviet symbols, red banners, Lenin statues in Eastern Europe
Eiffel Tower present = after 1889; London Eye after 2000; Sydney Opera House after 1973
baseline_tips: Find the NEWEST object in the picture. Old things survive for decades, new things can't appear early.
Cars are the best year clue in street scenes: date the newest car, then add a few years.
Location before year: script, driving side, plates and road markings narrow the country quickly.
Driving side: left in UK, Ireland, Japan, India, Australia, NZ, South Africa, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Hong Kong. Sweden switched to right in 1967.
In Cuba, Eastern Europe and Africa, cars are much older than the photo; adjust upward.
Clothing gives you the decade; hairstyles of young people are the most reliable.
Colour film in amateur photos: assume 1960s or later unless it looks like Kodachrome.
Shop signs: currencies, phone number formats (short numbers = old), web addresses (www = mid-1990s+), social media icons (2010+).
Military uniforms and helmets date wars precisely: WW1, WW2, Korea, Vietnam, etc.
Plates: the EU blue band means mid-1990s or later in most EU countries.
